n: Nahash, king of the Ammonites east of the Jordan, besieges the Israelite town of Jabesh-gilead. Outmatched, the townspeople offer to surrender and become his subjects.

f.g: Ammon was a nation east of the Jordan, descended from Lot.
A town in Gilead with old family ties to Benjamin.

n: Nahash's terms are brutal: he will gouge out every man's right eye to humiliate all Israel. Losing the right eye would also make men nearly useless as soldiers.

f.w: thrust out all your right eyes

n: The elders ask for a week's delay to seek help from the rest of Israel; if no one comes, they will surrender. Nahash's confidence shows how weak Israel seemed.

f.g: a period of delay or relief

n: The messengers arrive at Saul's town of Gibeah, and the people break down weeping when they hear the news.
Saul is still working as a farmer, coming in from the field with the oxen. Hearing the weeping, he asks what is wrong.
The Spirit of God comes powerfully on Saul, stirring righteous anger at this cruelty. Like the earlier judges, he is empowered to deliver Israel.

f.w: the Spirit of God came upon Saul

n: Saul cuts a pair of oxen into pieces and sends them throughout Israel with a warning: whoever doesn't follow Saul and Samuel will see the same done to his oxen. The fear of the Lord unites the people.
Saul musters a huge army at Bezek, with Judah counted separately — an early hint of the later divide between Judah and the northern tribes.

f.g: A site west of the Jordan, within marching distance of Jabesh-gilead.
Hebrew numbers like “thousand” may sometimes mean military units, so the totals may be smaller than they appear.

n: They send word to Jabesh-gilead: help will arrive by midday tomorrow. The besieged town rejoices.

f.w: by that time the sun be hot

n: The men of Jabesh tell the Ammonites they will come out tomorrow — a clever message that keeps the enemy off guard.
Saul divides his army into three groups and attacks in the early morning hours, catching the Ammonites by surprise. By noon the enemy is completely scattered.

f.g: the last part of the night, roughly 2–6 a.m.

n: Flush with victory, the people want to execute the men who had doubted Saul.
Saul shows mercy and gives credit to the Lord for the victory. This is Saul at his best — humble and gracious.
Samuel invites the people to Gilgal to renew and confirm the kingdom, now that Saul has proved himself.

f.g: An important site near Jericho where Israel first camped in Canaan.

n: At Gilgal the people publicly confirm Saul as king before the Lord, offer peace offerings, and celebrate together with great joy.

f.g: Sacrifices shared in a joyful meal, celebrating fellowship with God.
